problems.memo_sentence: "The authors propose a power-law amplitude estimation (AE) algorithm tailored for option pricing on NISQ devices, building on QFT-free AE by removing phase estimation and controlled-QFT while introducing a specific power-law schedule for Grover-type oracle calls and a fixed number of measurements per step."
problems.source_evidence: "Recently, an improved QFT-free AE algorithm, the power law AE algorithm, has been proposed in Ref. [19, 20]. Based on the required accuracy level, it leads to superior performance of quantum circuits with optimal selection of power-law scheduling."
problems.explanation: The memo presents the power-law schedule as a paper-specific design choice, but the paper frames power-law AE as an improved algorithm already proposed in prior references and only adapted here for option pricing. The contribution is application and simulation, not the original invention of the scheduling idea.

problems.memo_sentence: "The complete pricing circuit for their test instance uses three qubits—two for the discretized asset-price distribution and one ancilla to encode option returns—and is simulated in Qiskit."
problems.source_evidence: "To estimate the pricing of European call options, our quantum circuit employs three qubits, where two qubits load the probability distribution required for the European call option, and the last one is used to encode the option returns." / "Assume asset prices obey a normal distribution..." / "The possible asset prices [3.981, 6.001, 8.022, 10.042] are encoded by two qubits..."
problems.explanation: The memo correctly notes the three-qubit simulation, but it omits that the paper describes the instance as highly simplified and synthetic, with a discretized four-point price distribution and an approximate scaling choice. Those nearby caveats materially qualify the result.
